summary: Specifies extensions to IS-IS needed for link state routing of protocols running directly over Layer 2, with generic TLVs. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Lets a routing system that finds paths between routers also find paths for traffic that never uses internet addresses.

questions: what is the mac reachability tlv
subtitle: Two generic IS-IS building blocks that let a link state protocol carry Layer-2 port and MAC address information.

tldr.problem: Several systems route classical Layer-2 packets with a link state protocol, and each would otherwise need its own way to carry Layer-2 information in IS-IS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two generic IS-IS TLVs: the MT-PORT-CAP TLV (type 143) in Hello PDUs and the MAC-Reachability TLV (type 147) in Link State PDUs.
tldr.outcome: Technology-specific documents build on these TLVs. The RFC adds no new forwarding mechanism and no new security risk to IS-IS.

today: RFC 6165 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself leaves the use of its TLVs to the technology-specific documents.

sections.title: Why IS-IS Needs Layer-2 Extensions
sections.content:
Some systems, such as RBridges, 802.1aq (Shortest Path Bridging) and OTV, use Layer-2 addresses carried in a link state routing protocol to provide true Layer-2 routing. The protocol they use is Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS), as extended for IP in RFC 1195.

In almost all of these technologies, classical Layer-2 packets are encapsulated with an outer header, and that outer header is used to route the packet to its destination. The outer header format differs between the technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Several different mail systems want to use the same postal map, even though their envelopes look different. This document gives them a shared way to write on the map.

sections.title: What the RFC Covers and What It Leaves Out
sections.content:
Each Intermediate System (IS) advertises one or more Link State PDUs (LSPs). An LSP is a fixed header followed by a number of tuples, each made of a Type, a Length and a Value. These tuples are known as TLVs.

This document specifies a set of TLVs to add to IS-IS PDUs. They are generic Layer-2 additions. Specific ones, as needed, are defined in the IS-IS technology-specific extensions.

The RFC does not propose any new forwarding mechanism for the information it carries. It leaves it to the systems that use these extensions to explain how the information is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The document only says how to write the notes. It does not say what each mail system should do after reading them.

sections.title: The Port Capability TLV
sections.content:
The Multi-Topology-aware Port Capability TLV (MT-PORT-CAP) is IS-IS TLV type 143. It has a 1-byte Type, a 1-byte Length, and then a 2-byte word made of 4 reserved bits and a 12-bit Topology Identifier. Sub-TLVs of variable size follow.

  • Length is the total number of bytes in the value field, including the sub-TLVs.
  • The four reserved bits (R) MUST be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.
  • The Topology Identifier is the multi-topology ID of the topology being announced. Zero means the TLV carries base topology information.
  • The sub-TLVs are formatted as described in RFC 5305 and are defined in the technology-specific documents.

The TLV may occur multiple times and is carried within an IS-IS Hello (IIH) PDU.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a small card a router hands to its neighbors saying what a port can do. The details on the card are filled in by each mail system's own rules.

sections.title: The MAC-Reachability TLV
sections.content:
The MAC-Reachability TLV (MAC-RI) is IS-IS TLV type 147. After the Type and Length it holds a 2-byte Topology-id/Nickname, a 1-byte Confidence, 4 reserved bits with a 12-bit VLAN-ID, and then one or more 6-byte MAC addresses. The Length is 5 + 6*n bytes for n addresses.

  • Topology-id/Nickname carries a topology ID or a nickname, depending on the technology. Zero means the addresses are reachable across all topologies, or across all nicknames of the originating IS.
  • Confidence is an 8-bit level of confidence in the addresses. Its meaning is left to the protocol using the TLV. If unused, it MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.
  • VLAN-ID is a 12-bit VLAN identifier valid for all MAC addresses in the TLV, or zero if no VLAN is specified. The reserved bits MUST be zero and ignored on receipt.
  • Each MAC entry is a 48-bit address reachable from the IS announcing the TLV.

The TLV is carried in a standard LSP, and can appear multiple times in an LSP and in multiple LSPs. It MUST contain only unicast addresses. In most technologies, these entries translate into populating hardware with the addresses and the next hop derived from the advertising IS.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an address-book page: a router lists the device addresses it can reach, so other routers know whom to ask when a message is for one of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is brief on security: it adds no additional security risks to IS-IS, and it does not provide any additional security for IS-IS either.
sections.plainLanguage: The new notes are no riskier than the old ones, and they are no better protected either.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC defines two new IS-IS TLVs, listed in the IS-IS TLV codepoint registry: the Port-Capability TLV (type 143) and the MAC-Reachability TLV (type 147). The first appears in IIH PDUs. The second appears in LSPs. Neither is listed for sequence number PDUs (SNPs).
sections.plainLanguage: The two new kinds of note get official numbers in a public list, so nobody else reuses them.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Bytes in the value field, including sub-TLVs.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; sent as zero, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Topology Identifier
fields.desc: MT ID of the topology; zero means base topology.

fields.name: Topology-id/Nickname
fields.desc: Topology ID or nickname; zero means all.

fields.name: VLAN-ID
fields.desc: VLAN for the MACs that follow, or zero.

fields.name: MAC (1)
fields.desc: First 48-bit unicast MAC address (continues in the next 16 bits).
